start.text:
Triage handover:

Daniel Okafor, 34, a secondary school teacher, walks into the ED. He looks unwell — flushed, slightly hunched, and breathing a little harder than normal.

He tells triage: 'I've had a fever for three days and a really bad cough. I thought it was just a cold but I'm not getting better.'

Triage vitals:
HR 104 | BP 118/76 | RR 22 | Temp 38.9°C | SpO₂ 94% | Pain 4/10

He is placed in an acute bay. You are the ED registrar.

What is your first priority?

choices.text: Apply oxygen immediately (SpO₂ 94%), then take a focused history

effects.reason: Supplemental oxygen applied promptly for SpO₂ 94% — correct first step

choices.text: Take a focused history first before doing anything else

effects.reason: A patient with SpO₂ 94% and RR 22 should receive supplemental oxygen before you start the history

choices.text: Order a chest X-ray immediately — the clinical picture suggests a pulmonary cause

effects.reason: Chest X-ray ordered on first presentation — the most important initial test in undifferentiated fever + respiratory symptoms

choices.text: Draw bloods and request an FBC and CRP immediately

effects.reason: Bloods are appropriate but oxygen (SpO₂ 94%) and a CXR should take priority in a patient with fever and respiratory compromise

history-hub.text:
Daniel is cooperative. He has been sick for 3 days and is clearly not well.

You need a focused history. What do you want to explore?

choices.text: Respiratory symptoms — cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea
Systemic illness — fever pattern, rigors, sweats, myalgia, recent travel or contacts
Urinary symptoms — dysuria, frequency, loin pain (to screen for UTI/pyelonephritis)
Past medical history, medications, allergies, smoking
I have enough history — proceed to investigations

history-respiratory.text:
Daniel's respiratory history:

• Productive cough for 3 days — initially dry, now producing yellow-green sputum
• Right-sided sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing and coughing (pleuritic)
• Progressively worsening breathlessness — he's been winded walking to the bathroom
• No haemoptysis
• No wheeze (his asthma has been well-controlled for years)

This history is strongly suggestive of a lower respiratory tract infection — the pleuritic component and productive purulent sputum raise concern for pneumonia over viral bronchitis.

choices.text: Continue history

history-systemic.text:
Systemic history:

• Fever started 72 hours ago — initially 37.8°C, now 38.9°C at triage
• One episode of rigors on night 1
• Moderate sweats, particularly at night
• Significant myalgia and fatigue — he could not go to work yesterday
• No recent travel (never left the country)
• No sick contacts that he is aware of
• Loss of appetite, very poor oral intake over 2 days

No rash, no neck stiffness, no headache — making meningitis less likely. The fever duration and rigors are more characteristic of bacterial than purely viral illness.

choices.text: Continue history

history-urinary.text:
Urinary history:

• No dysuria
• No frequency or urgency
• No haematuria
• No loin or flank pain
• Urine looks normal coloured (though slightly dark — he admits he has been drinking less)

This makes a urinary source (UTI, pyelonephritis) significantly less likely. The absence of urinary symptoms in a male with fever and respiratory symptoms should shift your differential firmly toward a respiratory cause.

choices.text: Continue history

history-pmhx.text:
Past medical and social history:

• Mild intermittent asthma — last used salbutamol inhaler 3 months ago, well-controlled
• No other significant medical history
• Medications: salbutamol PRN (not taken recently)
• NKDA
• Smoker — 10 cigarettes/day for 12 years (approximately 6 pack-years)
• No alcohol or recreational drug use
• Lives alone in a flat; has not had flu vaccination this year

Smoking is a significant risk factor for pneumococcal pneumonia. His asthma, while mild, means respiratory compromise from pneumonia could escalate quickly.

choices.text: Continue history

exam-node.text:
Examination findings:

General: Alert but flushed, mildly distressed, splinting respirations on the right
Hands: No clubbing, no peripheral cyanosis
Neck: No cervical lymphadenopathy, no meningism

Chest:
• Inspection: Reduced expansion on the right
• Percussion: Dull in the right lower zone
• Auscultation: Bronchial breath sounds and increased vocal resonance in the right lower zone; fine inspiratory crackles at the right base; reduced air entry right lower lobe
• No wheeze

Abdomen: Soft, non-tender
No skin rash; no peripheral oedema

CLINICAL IMPRESSION: Right lower lobe consolidation — this is a classic examination for pneumonia. You need imaging to confirm.

choices.text: Proceed to investigations

investigation-hub.text:
You have enough clinical information to direct your investigation. Daniel remains on supplemental oxygen if you applied it. SpO₂ 94–96% on air.

Current working differential:
1. Community-acquired pneumonia (most likely)
2. Viral LRTI / bronchitis (possible but less likely given purulent sputum, rigors, exam)
3. Urinary source (very unlikely — no urinary symptoms)

What investigations do you want to order?

choices.text: Order a chest X-ray (PA erect)

effects.reason: Chest X-ray ordered — essential investigation in fever with respiratory symptoms

choices.text: Draw bloods: CBC, BMP, CRP, blood cultures ×2, procalcitonin, lactate

effects.reason: Comprehensive bloods drawn including blood cultures — essential workup for fever with possible bacterial infection
Blood cultures collected before antibiotics — correct practice that preserves microbiological data

choices.text: Order a urinalysis (to exclude urinary source)

effects.reason: Urinalysis has very low yield in a male with no urinary symptoms and a clear respiratory history — this delays the higher-priority workup

choices.text: Order a respiratory viral panel (influenza, COVID-19)

effects.reason: Viral panel is reasonable to help guide antibiotic stewardship — but should not delay CXR or bloods

choices.text: I have enough information — proceed to treatment decisions

urinalysis-result.text:
URINALYSIS RESULT
─────────────────────────────
Colour: Amber (concentrated)
Leukocyte esterase: NEGATIVE
Nitrites: NEGATIVE
WBC: 0–2 per high-power field (normal)
No casts, no blood, no protein of significance

This is a NORMAL urinalysis. There is no evidence of urinary tract infection.

As expected from the history, the urinary source has been excluded. The fever and systemic illness must be attributed elsewhere — your clinical suspicion should remain firmly on the respiratory tract.

choices.text: Return to investigations

viral-panel-result.text:
RESPIRATORY VIRAL PANEL (Multiplex PCR)
─────────────────────────────────────────
Influenza A: NEGATIVE
Influenza B: NEGATIVE
RSV: NEGATIVE
SARS-CoV-2: NEGATIVE
Rhinovirus/enterovirus: NEGATIVE

No common respiratory viruses detected.

This result further supports a bacterial aetiology. With purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, rigors, and now a negative viral panel, community-acquired pneumonia should be your leading diagnosis. A chest X-ray remains essential to confirm and characterise the disease.

choices.text: Return to investigations

bloods-result.text:
BLOOD RESULTS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CBC:
  WBC: 14.8 ×10⁹/L ↑ (ref 4–11) — Neutrophilia: 12.1 ×10⁹/L ↑
  Haemoglobin: 143 g/L (normal)
  Platelets: 198 ×10⁹/L (normal)

BMP:
  Na 136 mEq/L | K 3.9 mEq/L | Cr 104 μmol/L (mild ↑, likely pre-renal)
  Glucose 6.1 mmol/L

CRP: 142 mg/L ↑↑ (ref <5) — significantly elevated, bacterial infection likely
Procalcitonin: 2.8 ng/mL ↑ — supports bacterial source, consider sepsis workup
Lactate: 1.9 mmol/L (normal < 2.0) — No active tissue hypoperfusion at this time

Blood cultures: ×2 sets collected. Preliminary pending (final result 48–72h).

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INTERPRETATION:
Significant leukocytosis with neutrophilia and markedly elevated CRP strongly support a bacterial infection. PCT 2.8 ng/mL indicates a significant bacterial systemic response — this is NOT a simple viral illness.

Creatinine mildly elevated — likely dehydration (poor PO intake). Monitor closely.
Lactate is reassuring — no septic shock at this time — but this must be rechecked if he deteriorates.

choices.text: Order a chest X-ray now (if not already done)

effects.reason: Chest X-ray ordered — confirms the location and extent of suspected pneumonia

choices.text: I have enough — proceed to treatment

cxr-result.text:
CHEST X-RAY — PA ERECT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Lungs: RIGHT LOWER LOBE CONSOLIDATION — dense, homogeneous opacity in the right lower zone with air bronchograms visible. No pneumothorax. No pleural effusion (small effusion cannot be excluded on PA).
Left lung: clear
Heart size: Normal
Mediastinum: Normal
No bony abnormality

─────────────────────────────────────────────────
REPORT: Right lower lobe consolidation — consistent with lobar pneumonia.
Clinical correlation recommended.

This confirms your clinical diagnosis. Combined with:
• Fever, rigors, purulent sputum, pleuritic pain
• Examination: dullness, bronchial breathing, crackles in right lower zone
• CXR: right lower lobe consolidation

Diagnosis: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) — right lower lobe

Your next step is to assess severity and determine appropriate treatment and disposition.

effects.reason: CXR correctly identified right lower lobe consolidation — confirms CAP diagnosis

choices.text: Assess severity using CURB-65 scoring

effects.reason: CURB-65 severity assessment performed — guides admission vs discharge decision and antibiotic route

choices.text: I have enough — start treatment now

effects.reason: Formal severity scoring (CURB-65) is recommended and helps guide antibiotic route and disposition — skipping it is a minor omission

severity-assessment.text:
CURB-65 SEVERITY ASSESSMENT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
C — Confusion (new): No → 0
U — Urea >7 mmol/L: Borderline (creatinine mildly elevated, urea not checked) → 0
R — Respiratory rate ≥30/min: No (RR 22) → 0
B — BP systolic <90 or diastolic <60: No → 0
6 — Age ≥65: No → 0

CURB-65 score: 0

Score 0–1: Mild CAP — consider home treatment
Score 2: Moderate CAP — consider admission
Score ≥3: Severe CAP — hospital admission, ICU consideration

─────────────────────────────────────────────────
However — CURB-65 alone does not tell the full story:
• SpO₂ 94% on air — clinically significant hypoxaemia
• PCT 2.8, WBC 14.8, CRP 142 — significant systemic response
• Moderate dehydration
• Lives alone — poor social support if deteriorates
• Pre-existing asthma

Clinical judgment here is essential. A CURB-65 of 0 with SpO₂ 94% and these inflammatory markers warrants admission for IV antibiotics and monitoring — the score alone underestimates severity in this case.

choices.text: Proceed to treatment — decision is admission for IV antibiotics

treatment-decision.text:
Daniel is sitting in the acute bay. SpO₂ 95% on 2L O₂ via nasal prongs. He is comfortable enough to answer questions. RR 22.

You have confirmed:
• Right lower lobe pneumonia on CXR
• Significant inflammatory response (WBC 14.8, CRP 142, PCT 2.8)
• SpO₂ 94% on air → 95% on supplemental oxygen
• Mild renal impairment likely from dehydration

What is your treatment plan?

choices.text: IV amoxicillin-clavulanate + oral doxycycline, IV fluids, admit to medical ward

effects.reason: Correct dual-agent CAP regimen: beta-lactam + atypical cover (doxycycline) per IDSA/ATS guidelines. IV route appropriate for moderate severity + hypoxaemia.
IV fluids appropriate for dehydration and mild pre-renal creatinine elevation
Admission to medical ward — appropriate for moderate CAP with hypoxaemia

choices.text: Oral amoxicillin and discharge with GP follow-up (CURB-65 is 0 after all)
Give IV amoxicillin-clavulanate immediately — cultures can wait

effects.reason: Antibiotics administered — but blood cultures were not drawn first, which reduces the yield of microbiological data

choices.text: Hold antibiotics and await culture/viral results before committing to a treatment

treatment-given.text:
Treatment initiated:
• IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g q8h commenced
• Doxycycline 100mg BD PO (atypical cover: Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila)
• IV normal saline 1L over 4 hours
• Supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain SpO₂ ≥94%
• Analgesia: paracetamol 1g q6h for pleuritic pain and fever

Daniel is being prepared for admission to the respiratory medicine ward.

One final question before handover — is there anything else you need to address?

choices.text: Complete a clear handover to the ward team and document the management plan
Send a sputum sample for culture and gram stain before handover (good practice)

effects.reason: Sputum culture sent before handover — good antibiotic stewardship to enable de-escalation if culture returns with sensitivities

delayed-treatment-path.text:
One hour later — URGENT

The nurse calls you urgently. Daniel has deteriorated:

HR 122 | BP 96/58 | RR 28 | SpO₂ 88% on 2L O₂ | Temp 39.8°C

He is now confused — he cannot tell you the correct date.

He meets Sepsis-3 criteria:
• Suspected infection ✓
• Acute organ dysfunction: SOFA score increased ≥2
  — New confusion (CNS)
  — SpO₂ 88% despite supplemental O₂ (respiratory)
  — BP 96/58 (cardiovascular)

This patient is in SEPSIS. The delay in antibiotics has allowed systemic progression. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition.

You must act immediately.

choices.text: Sepsis bundle: blood cultures NOW, IV antibiotics, IV fluid bolus, high-flow O₂, urgent bloods, escalate

effects.reason: Antibiotics finally administered — but late recognition of sepsis has complicated the course
Blood cultures collected before antibiotics, even in the emergency

inappropriate-discharge.text:
Daniel is discharged with: oral amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 5 days and advice to return if he worsens.

He deteriorates at home overnight. His partner calls an ambulance at 03:00.

On arrival: HR 128 | BP 88/52 | RR 32 | SpO₂ 82% on air | Temp 40.1°C

He is admitted to the ICU with septic shock requiring non-invasive ventilation and vasopressors.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

CURB-65 = 0 does not always mean safe to discharge. Clinical context always overrides scoring tools:
• SpO₂ 94% on air is clinically significant and requires O₂ — this alone warrants admission for monitoring
• PCT 2.8 ng/mL indicates significant systemic bacterial response
• Mild renal impairment from dehydration requires IV fluids
• Lives alone — poor social support

Oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up are appropriate for mild CAP (CURB-65 0–1, no hypoxaemia, no comorbidities). This case did not meet that threshold.

abx-without-cultures-path.text:
IV amoxicillin-clavulanate is now running.

Nursing staff realise blood cultures were never drawn before the antibiotics started. They ask if you want them drawn now.

Note: Once antibiotics are in the bloodstream, blood cultures have significantly reduced yield. The opportunity to identify the causative organism has likely passed.

What do you do next?

choices.text: Draw blood cultures now anyway — even low yield is better than none

effects.reason: Blood cultures drawn after antibiotics are started — significantly reduced diagnostic yield

choices.text: Proceed with admission — add atypical cover (doxycycline) and IV fluids

effects.reason: IV fluids initiated — appropriate
Correct admission decision

sepsis-rescue.text:
The sepsis bundle is initiated promptly once you recognise the deterioration:
• Blood cultures ×2 drawn
• IV piperacillin-tazobactam commenced (broader spectrum given sepsis)
• IV doxycycline added for atypical cover
• 500 mL IV crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes
• High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
• Urgent repeat bloods including lactate (2.8 mmol/L — elevated)

Daniel is transferred to the High Dependency Unit (HDU) for monitoring.

Over the next 24 hours he improves: fevers resolve, SpO₂ stabilises on 4L O₂, blood pressure normalises. He is stepped down to the ward on day 2 and discharged on day 5.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Withholding antibiotics to await culture results is not justified in a patient with confirmed pneumonia, hypoxaemia, and elevated PCT. This approach caused preventable deterioration to sepsis. While the outcome was ultimately good, the delay added patient risk, ICU resource utilisation, and a longer hospital stay.

Key teaching: In moderate-to-severe CAP, antibiotics should be administered within 1 hour of diagnosis. Culture results inform de-escalation — not the initial decision.

outcome-excellent.text:
Daniel Okafor is admitted to the respiratory medicine ward under the general medicine team.

Treatment summary:
• IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g q8h
• Oral doxycycline 100mg BD
• IV normal saline 1L over 4 hours (for rehydration)
• Supplemental O₂ via nasal prongs, titrated ≥94%
• Paracetamol 1g q6h (antipyretic and analgesia)
• Thromboprophylaxis: low-molecular-weight heparin per protocol

Clinical course:
Day 1: Fevers reduce, feels slightly better
Day 2: Oral intake improving, SpO₂ 96% on air
Day 3: Apyrexial, SpO₂ 97% on room air, switched to oral antibiotics
Day 4: Discharged home with 5 days of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and doxycycline

Blood cultures: No growth after 5 days — common in CAP (organism identified in only ~25% of hospitalised CAP cases).

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Excellent work. This was a textbook approach to moderate community-acquired pneumonia:

✓ Early oxygen for SpO₂ 94%
✓ CXR confirming right lower lobe consolidation
✓ Blood cultures before antibiotics (antibiotic stewardship)
✓ Dual-agent therapy (beta-lactam + atypical cover)
✓ IV route for moderate severity + hypoxaemia
✓ IV fluids for mild pre-renal impairment
✓ Admission decision with clinical judgment beyond CURB-65

outcome-excellent-with-sputum.text:
Daniel is admitted to the respiratory medicine ward.

Sputum gram stain: Gram-positive diplococci — consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Sputum culture (day 2): S. pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin — de-escalation to IV amoxicillin alone on day 2.

Treatment course:
Day 1–2: IV amoxicillin-clavulanate + doxycycline
Day 2 onwards: IV amoxicillin (de-escalated based on sensitivities)
Day 4: Switched to oral amoxicillin and discharged

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Exceptional performance. Your sputum culture enabled antibiotic de-escalation — a hallmark of good antibiotic stewardship. This reduces adverse effects, Clostridioides difficile risk, and selection pressure for resistant organisms.

A small but meaningful clinical win that reflects the habits of an excellent clinician.
